title: A light of the nations (Isaiah 42:6)
hook: Israel is called to be "a light of the nations"

segments.voice: Yesterday, the nesher, wings as eagles: fly, run, walk and not faint. Your line was renew your strength. Did you pause before you were empty? Today, a calling with a lamp in it. Day seven hundred eighty-nine.

Chapter forty-two introduces a figure the book calls my servant, and before this chapter says the word light, we learn what this servant won't do. "He shall not cry, nor lift up, nor cause his voice to be heard in the street. A bruised reed shall he not break, and the smoking flax shall he not quench". No shouting. No snapping what's already cracked. No blowing out a flame that's nearly gone. Then, a few lines later, comes the calling.
screen: `A BRUISED REED. A SMOKING WICK.` → `NO SHOUTING IN THE STREET.` → `THEN, THE CALLING.`

segments.voice: Here it is, in verse six: "I the LORD have called thee in righteousness, and will hold thine hand." And then: I will give thee for a covenant of the people, for a light of the nations. The King James says Gentiles; the Hebrew word, goyim, means nations, and that's how the 1917 Jewish Publication Society translation renders it. So who is the servant? Jewish tradition hears the people Israel in these chapters, and we'll come back to the servant in a few days. Today, stay with the light. Look at what kind of light it is. It doesn't shout. It doesn't break the bruised reed. It doesn't snuff out the smoking wick. This is not a searchlight sweeping the streets. It's closer to a lamp in a window: it's simply there, and people find their way by it. And the next verse says what the light is for: "To open the blind eyes, to bring out the prisoners from the prison." Light, in Isaiah, is something that frees people. Jewish writers have taken this calling in different ways. Some hear it as a call to live by the Torah so faithfully that others notice. Some hear it as a call to justice, opening eyes and prison doors. Some hear it mainly as a promise held by God: I will hold thine hand. What they share is that the light is a calling, not a trophy. A lamp doesn't light itself to be admired. It lights the room.
screen: `NO SHOUTING, NO BREAKING THE REED.` · `I WILL HOLD THINE HAND.` · `GOYIM: THE NATIONS.` · `TO OPEN THE BLIND EYES.` · then, large: `A LIGHT OF THE NATIONS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: be a light for one person. Settle, and breathe. Let one person come to mind who is a bit of a bruised reed right now, cracked but not broken, or a wick that's burning low. Don't plan anything loud. Ask the quiet question: what small thing would help them see their way today? A word of credit. A door held open. An answer to the message they sent. Choose one. If you pray, you can hold the verse: I will hold thine hand. The bell holds the time.
A light of the nations. From Isaiah forty-two: a servant called to be a covenant of the people and a light that opens eyes. Today's word.
screen: `A LIGHT OF THE NATIONS — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: a light to the nations. Today, do the quiet thing you chose, for the one person, and don't break anything that's already bruised. Day seven hundred eighty-nine.

howItsDone: Isaiah 42 is read in synagogue as a haftarah, and the phrase a light to the nations is used in Jewish teaching for the calling of the people Israel, understood in different ways by different communities.

original.note: Hebrew: a light of the nations, from Isaiah 42:6.

trapdoor: what you thought: a call to be famous for being good.
what it means: a quiet light, like a lamp in a window, that opens eyes and frees people.
what a scholar hears: the King James says Gentiles; the Hebrew goyim means nations, and the same chapter says the servant won't break a bruised reed.
